brand.title: ESourceAIG (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Project Management - Bid to close

questions.question: What are the six phases of the Pennebaker project lifecycle in order?
choices: Bid Opportunity, Estimate and Bid, Award and Setup, Procurement and Planning, Execution and Management, Closeout
Bid Opportunity, Award and Setup, Estimate and Bid, Procurement and Planning, Execution and Management, Closeout
Estimate and Bid, Bid Opportunity, Award and Setup, Procurement and Planning, Execution and Management, Closeout
Bid Opportunity, Estimate and Bid, Procurement and Planning, Award and Setup, Execution and Management, Closeout
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly right—these six phases always occur in this order and every project moves through all of them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The sequence matters because handoffs depend on phases happening in the right order. Review Slide 3 to lock in the correct sequence.

questions.question: Who is responsible for managing the bid calendar and due dates?
choices: The PM
Brandy, the Bid Coordinator
Jay and the Estimating Team
Contract Administration
questions.feedback_correct: That's correct—Brandy manages the bid calendar and due dates as part of the intake process.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The PM does not manage the bid calendar intake. Brandy handles that role, and the PM enters the picture later during the pre-bid walkthrough.

questions.question: What is a submittal and who obtains it?
choices: A signed contract document that the PM must obtain from the client
A vendor or manufacturer document proving that equipment or material matches the design, obtained by the PM
A purchase order issued by Jasmine to confirm material delivery
A formal request for information sent to the architect when drawings are unclear
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—a submittal is the vendor's proof that what they are providing matches the design, and the PM gets it and sends it for approval.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A submittal comes from the vendor, not the client, and the PM's job is to obtain it, review it, and send it to the owner or architect for approval.

questions.question: Which two estimating pathways exist, and what determines which one you use?
choices: Pathway A is for direct-request work; Pathway B is for larger scopes with piping takeoff
Pathway A is for larger scopes or piping takeoff; Pathway B is for direct-request work where a client comes to you
Both pathways use Trimble AutoBid; the difference is whether the client approves the estimate first
Pathway A requires a formal Gantt chart; Pathway B is mental planning only
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—Pathway A goes to the estimating team for larger or piping scopes, and Pathway B is PM-led for direct-request client work.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The pathways are determined by project scope and complexity. Pathway A involves the formal estimating team and Trimble AutoBid; Pathway B is PM-led with simpler tools.

questions.question: What is a documented gap in the current PO request process?
choices: There is no standard submittal checklist for site walkthroughs
There is no formal purchase approval step or verified budget check before a PO request is submitted
There is no formal EAC update process at the PM level
There is no standardized calculation method for percent complete
questions.feedback_correct: Right—there is currently no verified budget check or formal approval step before a PO request goes in, which is a real process gap.
questions.feedback_incorrect: This specific gap is about the PO request workflow. There is no controlled budget check before the request is submitted, so PMs must document carefully as a workaround.

questions.question: When a bid is won and a letter of intent is issued, whose responsibility is it to handle the formal contract and bonding?
choices: The PM takes over immediately and signs the contract
Contract Administration handles the formal contract, bonding, and NTP processing
The Bid Coordinator finalizes all agreements
Operations Leadership approves and signs all contracts
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—Contract Administration owns the formal contract, bonding, and NTP processing when a bid is won.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The PM does not sign contracts—that is explicitly outside the PM's authority. Contract Administration handles that responsibility.

questions.question: What do WIP and EAC stand for, and what is their function in project management?
choices: WIP is Weekly Invoicing Progress and EAC is Earned Account Code; they track billing
WIP is Work in Progress (financial snapshot of earned versus spent) and EAC is Estimate at Completion (updated cost prediction); together they are an early warning system
WIP is Weekly Installation Plan and EAC is Equipment and Closeout; they track field scheduling
WIP is Worksite Input Process and EAC is Expense Authorization Code; they control spending limits
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—WIP and EAC together give you an early warning about project profitability before losses become final.
questions.feedback_incorrect: WIP and EAC are financial indicators, not administrative codes. WIP shows how much you have earned versus spent, and EAC predicts your final project cost—both critical for catching problems early.

questions.question: Why does the course emphasize that PMs should name the gaps in the current process and work around them carefully?
choices: Because the gaps are the PM's fault and need to be fixed immediately
Because the process is perfect and there are no real gaps to worry about
Because the gaps are real, not a weakness, and separating strong PMs is the ability to recognize gaps and compensate for them carefully
Because gaps only exist in the Closeout phase and can be ignored until the end
questions.feedback_correct: That's right—the course is honest about where the process has real holes, and strong PM practice means recognizing them and working around them, not pretending they do not exist.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course treats gaps as real current-state realities, not failures. A strong PM at Pennebaker acknowledges gaps and builds safeguards, like documenting PO requests when budget control is loose.

questions.question: You are assigned a direct-request job where the client comes to you with a specific need, no formal bid. Which estimating pathway do you follow, and what is your first action?
choices: Pathway A; send the work to Jay and the estimating team to run in Trimble AutoBid
Pathway B; visit the site, take detailed notes and photos, and contact subcontractors for pricing while copying Jasmine
Pathway A; build a simple AutoBid symbol and cost entry estimate yourself
Pathway B; request a formal Gantt chart in Microsoft Project before any estimate work begins
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—Pathway B is PM-led for direct-request work, and your first action is the site visit with documentation and subcontractor outreach.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Direct-request work follows Pathway B, which is PM-led, not Pathway A. Your job is to gather field intelligence, document it, get subcontractor quotes, and build the estimate yourself.

questions.question: What is the current state of Closeout documentation at Pennebaker, and why does this create risk for the PM?
choices: Closeout is fully documented with standardized checklists for all steps from punch list to project archival
Closeout is the least documented phase; steps like punch list, retainage, and job cost reconciliation are not formally described, creating ambiguity about who owns what
Closeout is handled entirely by Contract Administration, so the PM has no responsibility in that phase
Closeout requires a formal Gantt chart and Microsoft Project schedule before any work can begin
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—Closeout is the least documented phase and that gap means the PM must be extra clear about ownership and sequence to avoid final-phase surprises.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Closeout is actually the least documented phase, not the most. This is a real gap that affects billing, retainage, warranty, and final reconciliation—all PM responsibilities that need clear process.
